title: PureSuperQMA(exp) = BellPureSymQMA(poly) = QMA via Dimension-Free Bosonic Argmax
authors: William Gay, Fernando Granha Jeronimo, Lenny Liu, Itai Leigh, Pei Wu, Haochen Xu
abstract: Pure-state consistency problems naturally lead to quantum proof systems in which a single pure witness must satisfy many acceptance constraints. The corresponding class $\mathsf{PureSuperQMA}$ was previously known to lie between $\mathsf{QMA}$ and $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$, and Kamminga and Rudolph (ITCS'26) conjectured that both containments are strict. In this paper, we prove the following surprising complexity collapses $$   \mathsf{QMA} = \mathsf{PureSuperQMA} = \mathsf{PureSuperQMA}(\text{exp}) = \mathsf{BellPureSymQMA}(\text{poly}) $$ Here $\mathsf{PureSuperQMA}(\text{exp})$ allows exponentially many checks which are uniformly indexed and efficiently generated, while requiring an inverse-polynomial violation margin and an inverse-polynomial fraction of violated checks for the NO cases. $\mathsf{BellPureSymQMA}(\text{poly})$ is a related model that requires the prover to give the verifier polynomially many copies of a pure state, which the verifier measures separately with logarithmic output length for each local measurement, before processing the outcomes jointly.   The main technical ingredient is a dimension-free stability bound for symmetric tensor states. Our simulations use polynomially many witness registers and combine a random-pair SWAP test with a permutation-invariant lift of the original verification procedure. The key step is to show that, on the symmetric subspace, the extremal verification value is close to that of some tensor-power witness with dimension-independent error. Applying this argument to the two verification models yields both simulations. As a consequence, exact $k$-local pure-state consistency is $\mathsf{QMA}$-complete for every fixed $k\ge2$, and so are the corresponding exact bosonic and fermionic pure $N$-representability problems.
summary: This paper proves a major complexity collapse showing that several advanced quantum proof systems, including PureSuperQMA and BellPureSymQMA, are all equivalent in computational power to QMA. This equivalence implies that checking for exact local consistency in pure quantum states is as hard as the general QMA-complete problems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of pure-state consistency problems, which are related to determining if a set of local quantum states can arise from a single global state.
main_result: The authors prove a significant complexity collapse: QMA = PureSuperQMA = PureSuperQMA(exp) = BellPureSymQMA(poly), establishing that exact k-local pure-state consistency is QMA-complete.
method: The proof relies on applying a dimension-free stability bound for symmetric tensor states to simulate the complex verification procedures of PureSuperQMA(exp) and BellPureSymQMA(poly) into the standard QMA framework.
model_or_system: The models are quantum proof systems ($	ext{PureSuperQMA}$, $	ext{BellPureSymQMA}$) used to characterize the difficulty of quantum marginal problems (local-to-global consistency checks) for pure states.
key_observables: The extremal verification value, the gap size between YES/NO instance probabilities, and the total variation distance between probability distributions.
important_parameters: The number of local measurements ($k$), the witness size (polynomial vs. exponential), and the violation margin ($\epsilon$) and fraction ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the validity of dimension-free stability bounds for symmetric tensor states and relies on techniques from quantum information theory and harmonic analysis.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical motivation (CLDM/quantum marginal problem), defines the complexity classes ($	ext{PureSuperQMA}$, etc.), and then proceeds through technical sections detailing the dimension-free stability bound, followed by the explicit simulations proving the stated complexity equalities.
why_interesting: The result provides a deep connection between fundamental problems in quantum many-body physics (like N-representability) and the established complexity class QMA, suggesting that these physical constraints are computationally hard.
